name: Unicode-level sanitization: tag characters, bidi controls, zero-width characters and homoglyphs. The standards layer: Unicode Technical Standard #39 Unicode Security Mechanisms (UTS39), which defines the confusables data and the skeleton/bidiSkeleton algorithms and the restriction-level and identifier-profile machinery; Unicode Technical Standard #55 Unicode Source Code Handling (UTS55), whose section 5.1 covers confusability mitigation diagnostics; Unicode Standard Annex #9 the Bidirectional Algorithm, whose higher-level protocol HL4 is the sanctioned tailoring point; Unicode Standard Annex #15 Normalization Forms (NFC/NFD/NFKC/NFKD); Unicode Standard Annex #31 Identifier and Pattern Syntax. The attack literature: Trojan Source (CVE-2021-42574 bidi reordering, CVE-2021-42694 homoglyph identifiers); ASCII smuggling via the Unicode Tags block U+E0000-U+E007F; variation-selector smuggling (U+E0100-U+E01EF); zero-width binary encoding; emoji and ZWJ-sequence injection; Reverse CAPTCHA: Evaluating LLM Susceptibility to Invisible Unicode Instruction Injection (arXiv:2603.00164); the Cloud Security Alliance research note on hidden Unicode instruction injection in agent skills, tool descriptions and MCP servers. Classification: OWASP LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection, whose 2025 revision explicitly names invisible Unicode payloads.
kind: Standards (UTS39, UTS55, UAX9, UAX15, UAX31) plus a body of research results and CVEs, plus implementations (ICU's confusables and normalisation, Python unicodedata, the confusable_homoglyphs and similar libraries, linters and scanners such as Cisco's skill-scanner). Not a single tool; a layer of the pipeline with a well-specified standards basis and a poorly-specified deployment practice.
maturity: The standards are mature and stable -- UTS39 has existed for two decades, confusables data ships with every ICU release, and normalisation is bedrock. The APPLICATION of them to LLM input pipelines is new and unsettled: the attack techniques are two to five years old in the source-code context (Trojan Source, 2021) and one to two years old in the LLM context, and there is no standard sanitisation profile for LLM ingestion, no consensus on what to strip, and no widely-deployed library that does it correctly. Practitioner posts and vendor scanners are filling the gap ad hoc. This is the single most mature standards foundation in this research set attached to the least mature practice.
license: Unicode standards and data files (confusables.txt, the UCD) are under the Unicode licence, which is permissive and explicitly permits use and redistribution -- no obstacle. ICU is under the Unicode licence. Python's unicodedata is stdlib. The various homoglyph libraries are MIT/BSD-family. Everything needed here is freely usable.
keeps_and_discards: A Unicode sanitiser sits between capture and use and decides which code points survive. The decision is genuinely consequential in both directions and the naive version is wrong. WHAT SHOULD GO, with high confidence: the Tags block U+E0000-U+E007F, which has no legitimate modern use (it was deprecated for language tagging, and its only current sanctioned role is inside emoji flag sequences, which are a bounded and enumerable exception); bidi FORMATTING controls used for override -- U+202A-U+202E and the isolate controls U+2066-U+2069 -- when they appear unbalanced or in contexts that do not need them; and the deprecated interlinear annotation characters. WHAT IS DANGEROUS TO STRIP NAIVELY: zero-width characters, because U+200D ZERO WIDTH JOINER and U+200C ZERO WIDTH NON-JOINER are SEMANTICALLY REQUIRED in Indic, Persian and Arabic orthography and in emoji ZWJ sequences -- stripping them corrupts text in a large fraction of the world's writing systems, and this is the single most common error in published sanitisers. U+FEFF (byte order mark used as zero-width no-break space) and U+200B ZERO WIDTH SPACE are safer to strip since they carry no orthographic role, but even they appear as legitimate soft-break hints. WHAT MUST NOT BE STRIPPED BUT MUST BE DETECTED: homoglyphs, since a Cyrillic 'а' is a legitimate character in Cyrillic text and only suspicious when mixed into a Latin string -- the correct treatment is script-mixing detection, not substitution. The general rule that falls out: normalise and DETECT rather than silently strip, because silent stripping is itself a fidelity loss that is invisible downstream, and because the detection result is the thing worth recording.
structure_preserved: Sanitisation operates on code point sequences and preserves all document structure. Two structural interactions matter. First, normalisation form changes the byte sequence, so any content hash, trie key or address computed over unnormalised text is invalidated by normalising later -- normalisation must happen at a single defined point in the pipeline and identically on every path, or the same text produces two different keys (this is the same hazard flagged in item 22). Second, bidi controls have DOCUMENT-SCOPE effects in some contexts: an unterminated override can affect the display of everything after it, so a control character inside one node can change how a sibling renders, which means node-local sanitisation is not sufficient for display correctness even though it is sufficient for content correctness.
interactive_elements: Directly relevant in one specific way: invisible characters hide well inside the ATTRIBUTES that describe controls -- aria-label, title, alt, placeholder, value -- which are short, rarely inspected, and read verbatim by accessibility tooling and by any tag-plus-interactivity representation. A button whose accessible name contains a tag-block-encoded instruction looks like an ordinary button in every representation. Attribute values must be screened on the same footing as text nodes, and this is easy to overlook because attributes are usually treated as metadata rather than as content.
layout_awareness: None required, and this is the property that makes this item so valuable to a layout-blind design. Every Unicode-level concealment technique is detectable from the CODE POINTS ALONE -- no rendering, no computed style, no geometry. Tag characters, variation selectors, zero-width sequences, bidi controls and script mixing are all properties of the string. Bidi is the interesting edge case: its EFFECT is visual, so knowing exactly what a human sees requires running the bidirectional algorithm, but detecting that override controls are PRESENT requires only a scan, and UTS39's bidiSkeleton makes the visual-order comparison computable without rendering. So the entire class is inside the fold, which is the sharpest contrast with the rendering-based concealment class of item 13.
javascript_required: No. Sanitisation and detection are pure string operations, applicable to fetched bytes, to a stored capture or to live DOM text equally.
evaluation_method: Three traditions. (1) STANDARDS CONFORMANCE: UTS39 defines skeleton() and bidiSkeleton() precisely and ships confusables.txt as data, so 'are these two strings confusable' is a decidable question with a reference implementation in ICU -- an unusually strong foundation. (2) VULNERABILITY DISCLOSURE: Trojan Source established the attack empirically by demonstrating working exploits against multiple compilers and code-review tools, which is a proof-of-existence method rather than a prevalence measurement. (3) MODEL SUSCEPTIBILITY TESTING, the newest and the one that produces the numbers below: encode an instruction invisibly, embed it in otherwise benign input, present it to models under controlled conditions, and grade whether the model decoded and complied. Reverse CAPTCHA does this carefully with a factorial design -- two encoding schemes, four hint levels, two payload types, with and without tool access -- and grades thousands of outputs. What is entirely MISSING from all three: any prevalence measurement of Unicode-level concealment on the real web. Item 13's large-scale study explicitly could not find obfuscated or encoded injections because its detector was keyword-based over visible text, so the fraction of real-world injections using Unicode concealment rather than CSS concealment is unknown. That is the single most important missing number for deciding how much this class matters relative to the rendering-based class.
corpus_size_and_origins: Standards data: confusables.txt maps 6,565 characters to visual equivalents, which is the reference corpus for homoglyph detection and is curated by the Unicode consortium rather than sampled. Reverse CAPTCHA: 270 test cases spanning two encoding schemes, four hint levels and two payload types, expanded across models, tool conditions and encodings to 8,308 graded outputs, with each condition run at least three times and cell sizes between 60 and 150 repetitions -- a properly powered design, and synthetic by construction. Trojan Source: demonstrations across a handful of major compilers and languages. NO WEB CORPUS EXISTS for this phenomenon. Nothing here tells you how often a real page contains a tag-block payload, and the one web-scale injection study (item 13, 1.2 billion URLs) was structurally unable to detect them. Reach limitation on the model-susceptibility numbers specifically: five frontier hosted models from two providers, no open-weight or small local models tested, which is precisely the model class this project uses.
reported_precision_recall: MODEL SUSCEPTIBILITY, from Reverse CAPTCHA, with denominators (8,308 graded outputs, cells of 60-150 repetitions, five models, two encodings -- zero-width binary using U+200B for 0 and U+200C for 1, and Tags-block mapping where each ASCII character maps to U+E0000 plus its code point). WITH TOOL ACCESS ENABLED, compliance with the invisible instruction: Claude Sonnet 4 47.4%, Claude Opus 4 30.1%, Claude Haiku 4.5 25.0%, GPT-5.2 10.3%, GPT-4o-mini 0.9%. WITHOUT TOOLS, all models showed compliance at or below 16.9%. Two readings matter. First, the absolute rates are high -- an order of magnitude above the 0.2-8.0% compliance rates measured for visible-text injections in item 13 -- which suggests invisible encoding is substantially MORE effective at eliciting compliance than plain hidden text, plausibly because the decoding act itself frames the content as a puzzle to solve rather than as page content to summarise. Second, TOOL ACCESS ROUGHLY TRIPLES SUSCEPTIBILITY for the most affected model (47.4% with tools versus at most 16.9% without), which is directly relevant to any agentic design and is the study's most actionable finding. CONFUSABLES: confusables.txt covers 6,565 characters. TROJAN SOURCE: CVE-2021-42574 (bidi) and CVE-2021-42694 (homoglyph identifiers), affecting the Unicode bidirectional algorithm through version 14.0 and demonstrated against multiple compilers; no rate is meaningful for a vulnerability class. NOT AVAILABLE: any real-world prevalence figure, any measurement on small open-weight models, and any measured false-positive rate for a sanitiser applied to real multilingual web text -- that last is the number a deployment needs most and nobody has it.
independent_oracle: Strong and unusual: UTS39's skeleton algorithm gives a decidable, standards-defined answer to whether two strings are confusable, computed by a reference implementation (ICU) maintained independently of any consumer, so 'is this a homoglyph attack' has an external oracle rather than a heuristic. Similarly, whether a string contains code points from the Tags block is a decidable set-membership test with no judgement involved. For the MODEL susceptibility question the oracle is behavioural grading of outputs, which is human or model-assisted and weaker. The strength of the character-level oracle is the reason this whole class is worth attacking first: it is the one part of injection defence where detection is exact rather than probabilistic.
evidence_independence: Good. The Unicode standards are consortium documents with no vendor interest in the outcome. Trojan Source was independent academic security research (Cambridge) that triggered coordinated disclosure and independent vendor responses (Red Hat's advisory among them), which is corroboration by an unrelated party. Reverse CAPTCHA is academic and tests five models from two providers, neither of which authored it. The weaker material is the practitioner and vendor layer -- blog posts describing sanitisers, security-product scanners, and the CSA research note -- which is directionally consistent but is not measurement and in several cases propagates the naive strip-all-zero-width advice that would corrupt Indic and Arabic text. Treat the standards and the two research results as evidence, and the practitioner sanitiser recipes as untested suggestions.
page_archetype_coverage: Unmeasured, since no web-corpus study exists. Mechanically, the exposure concentrates wherever text is user-supplied and rendered without normalisation: forums, comment threads, product reviews, job listings, profile fields, wiki content -- the same archetypes item 13 identifies as high-risk for visible injections, for the same reason. It also concentrates in a channel item 13 did not consider and the CSA note emphasises: TOOL AND SKILL DESCRIPTIONS, MCP server manifests, and any machine-readable text a system ingests as configuration, which for this project maps onto anything the sensor reads as instruction-adjacent metadata rather than as page prose. Documentation pages are again the false-positive hazard, since pages about Unicode security legitimately contain the very code points a scanner looks for.
script_and_locale_behaviour: This IS the field, and getting it wrong is the primary failure mode of every naive implementation. The critical facts. (1) U+200D ZWJ and U+200C ZWNJ are ORTHOGRAPHICALLY REQUIRED in Devanagari and other Indic scripts (controlling conjunct formation), in Persian and Arabic (controlling joining behaviour), and in emoji ZWJ sequences; stripping them is data corruption affecting hundreds of millions of users' text, and it is what most published LLM sanitisers do. (2) Bidi controls are REQUIRED for correct display of mixed-direction text -- an Arabic or Hebrew page legitimately contains isolates and embeddings, so blanket removal breaks RTL content; UAX9's HL4 higher-level-protocol tailoring is the sanctioned way to constrain them (for example, requiring balance within a node and terminating unbalanced controls at boundaries) rather than deleting them. (3) NFKC normalisation, widely recommended for LLM pipelines, is LOSSY in ways that matter beyond security: it collapses full-width and half-width forms, converts ligatures, decomposes superscripts, and destroys distinctions that are meaningful in Japanese and in mathematical text -- so NFKC is appropriate for a COMPARISON key and inappropriate as the stored form. NFC is the right stored form (it is the web's default and what DOM comparisons assume); NFKC belongs in the skeleton used for confusability checks only. (4) Homoglyph detection must be script-aware: mixed-script strings are the signal, and a monoscript Cyrillic string is not an attack. UTS39's restriction levels formalise exactly this and should be used rather than reinvented. The overall conclusion is that a structure-agnostic, script-invariant sanitiser is achievable but only by following UTS39's design rather than by ad-hoc stripping, and that almost every published LLM-oriented recipe fails this test.
leaks_outward: Nothing outward. Worth noting the inverse channel: invisible characters are a covert EXFILTRATION medium as well as an injection medium -- a model induced to echo tag-block characters can encode data in its output invisibly, and any pipeline that stores or forwards model output verbatim carries that channel. Screening OUTPUT for invisible code points is as important as screening input and is almost never done.
mechanism_detectability: Not applicable to the page. Relevant in the reverse direction and it connects to item 13's finding that thousands of deployed injections exist to identify AI readers: an invisible instruction is a near-perfect reverse-CAPTCHA, invisible to a human and legible to a model, so complying with one identifies the reader as a model with high confidence. The Reverse CAPTCHA paper's title reflects exactly this framing. A sensor that normalises invisible characters out before the model sees them is therefore protecting its own unobservability as well as its integrity.
countermeasures: A defensible profile, ordered and with the traps named. (1) NORMALISE TO NFC AT A SINGLE DEFINED POINT, applied identically on every ingestion path and before any hashing or key construction. Store NFC. (2) STRIP OR REJECT the Tags block U+E0000-U+E007F outright, excepting the enumerated emoji tag sequences; this block has no other legitimate modern use and it is the primary ASCII-smuggling vehicle. (3) STRIP variation selectors U+E0100-U+E01EF when they do not follow a base character that takes them, since a run of them is a smuggling signature and an isolated one is meaningless. (4) DETECT AND FLAG, DO NOT BLINDLY STRIP, zero-width characters: remove U+200B and U+FEFF (no orthographic role), but PRESERVE U+200C and U+200D and instead flag anomalous runs -- a legitimate ZWJ appears between two joining characters, whereas a binary-encoded payload appears as a long run of alternating zero-width characters in a context with no joining script, which is a mechanical, script-aware test. (5) BIDI: detect unbalanced overrides and isolates, terminate them at node boundaries per UAX9's HL4 tailoring rather than deleting them, and flag any node whose bidiSkeleton differs materially from its logical order. (6) HOMOGLYPHS: compute UTS39 skeletons and apply restriction levels; flag mixed-script strings rather than substituting characters. (7) RECORD EVERY ACTION as a per-node flag with what was removed and how much -- silent sanitisation is a silent fidelity loss and violates the same principle the project applies elsewhere. (8) SCREEN OUTPUT as well as input. (9) The most robust place is TOKENISER-LEVEL filtering, since it prevents the model from perceiving the content at all, but it requires care to preserve legitimate uses and is not available for a hosted model; for a local model it is achievable and is the strongest version of this defence.
measured_fidelity_cost: Not measured anywhere, and it is the field's most glaring gap. No study reports the false-positive rate of a Unicode sanitiser against real multilingual web text -- how often a correct Devanagari conjunct, a Persian word, an emoji ZWJ sequence, or a legitimately mixed-script string (a Latin brand name in a Cyrillic sentence, a Japanese page quoting an English term) is flagged or corrupted. Given that the naive recipe strips exactly the characters those languages need, the cost of the widely-advised profile is plausibly severe and entirely unquantified. The measurement is straightforward and should be run on the project's own corpus: apply the profile, count modified nodes by script, and inspect a sample. Against a control of no sanitisation, the fidelity cost is the modification rate; against a control of naive stripping, the benefit of the script-aware profile is the difference in that rate on non-Latin content.
gate_state_at_capture: Not applicable directly. One connection: user-generated content, which is where Unicode payloads concentrate, is disproportionately behind authentication, and item 13's corpus explicitly under-represents authenticated content -- so the unmeasured prevalence is concentrated in exactly the pages a session-based sensor reads.
determinism: Fully deterministic. Normalisation, code-point set membership, skeleton computation and script detection are pure functions with standards-defined algorithms and reference implementations. This is the most deterministic defence available anywhere in this research set and it is the strongest argument for doing this layer first: unlike every content-level or model-level defence, its behaviour is exactly specifiable, exactly reproducible, and exactly testable.
determinism_across_versions: Drifts slowly and predictably with the Unicode version. confusables.txt gains entries, new code points are assigned, normalisation is stable by policy (Unicode guarantees normalisation stability for already-assigned characters, which is a strong and deliberate commitment) but new characters change what NFKC does to previously-unassigned code points. Script property assignments can change. Practical rule: pin the Unicode/ICU version, record it in the capture metadata, and treat a Unicode version bump as a re-baselining event for any stored skeleton or normalised key. Note the contrast with everything else in this research set -- a versioned, published data file with a stability policy is about as good as cross-version determinism gets.
reproducibility: Excellent. Given the same input bytes and the same pinned Unicode version, a sanitiser's output and its flags are exactly reproducible, forever. The stored capture plus the recorded Unicode version is sufficient to re-derive every decision. This makes Unicode screening the one part of an injection-defence pipeline that can be made a reproducible pure function, which is a strong argument for placing as much of the defence here as the threat model allows.
failure_modes: (1) NAIVE ZERO-WIDTH STRIPPING corrupting Indic, Persian, Arabic and emoji text -- the dominant real failure of deployed sanitisers, and it is silent. (2) NFKC AS THE STORED FORM, destroying full-width/half-width and ligature distinctions that matter in Japanese and in typography. (3) NORMALISATION APPLIED INCONSISTENTLY across pipeline paths, producing duplicate keys for identical text (the trie-key hazard from item 22). (4) SCREENING TEXT NODES BUT NOT ATTRIBUTES, leaving aria-label, title, alt and placeholder unscreened. (5) SCREENING INPUT BUT NOT OUTPUT, leaving an invisible exfiltration channel open. (6) PER-NODE SCREENING DEFEATED BY SPLITTING a payload across adjacent nodes, so that no single node contains a suspicious run -- the direct analogue of the cross-node evasion in item 13 and equally real here. (7) UNBALANCED BIDI CONTROLS whose effects cross node boundaries, so node-local treatment leaves display-order anomalies. (8) FALSE POSITIVES on documentation about Unicode security. (9) VERSION SKEW between the sanitiser's Unicode data and the browser's, so the two disagree about what is a valid character or which script it belongs to.
failure_visibility: Silent by default in both directions, which is why the recording discipline matters more here than the stripping. An unsanitised payload passes through invisibly; an over-aggressive sanitiser corrupts text invisibly. Neither raises an error. The remedy is mandatory and cheap: every sanitisation action must produce a per-node record of what class of code point was removed or flagged and how many, attached to the address, so that both an attack and an over-correction are visible after the fact. Given that the underlying operations are exact, there is no excuse for a probabilistic or unrecorded outcome at this layer.
scale_limits: Trivial. Normalisation and set-membership scanning are linear in text length with small constants; skeleton computation is more expensive because it consults a table and, for bidiSkeleton, may need the bidirectional algorithm -- UTS39 notes bidiSkeleton is costlier than internalSkeleton but provides a fast path: when the direction is LTR and the string contains no characters of bidi class R or AL, bidiSkeleton equals internalSkeleton. So the expensive path is taken only for strings that actually contain RTL characters, which is a well-designed optimisation and means the whole layer is affordable inline on every node.
delta_cost_model: Excellent fit with an incremental design: screening is per-string and content-local, so a changed text node costs the node and unchanged nodes retain their recorded verdict. The fast path above keeps the constant small. What falls OUTSIDE the per-change bound, and must be named: (1) CROSS-NODE PAYLOADS, where a sequence split across siblings is invisible to any node-local scan -- the fundamental evasion and the one that makes an exception-free guarantee impossible; (2) UNBALANCED BIDI CONTROLS whose effect extends past the node containing them, so display-order correctness is not node-local even though content screening is; (3) a UNICODE VERSION BUMP, which invalidates every recorded verdict and requires an O(store) rescan -- rare but total; (4) ATTRIBUTE screening, which is per-attribute and must be driven by attribute mutation records, not only by characterData records; (5) OUTPUT screening, which is per-generation and outside the DOM delta entirely; (6) content that never enters the fold -- closed shadow roots, canvas text, cross-origin frames -- which is unscreenable by construction and belongs in the declared-incompleteness set.
reanchoring_stability: Directly implicated through normalisation. If content hashes are used for re-anchoring (as item 23 recommends), the hash must be computed over a canonically normalised form or the same visible text in NFC and NFD produces different hashes and every re-anchor fails. Conversely, normalising after the key is built silently changes the key. The rule is: normalise once, at ingestion, to NFC, before any hash or key is computed, and record the Unicode version. This is a small detail with a large failure mode and it is the kind of thing that produces an unexplained re-anchor failure rate months later.
adversarial_exposure: This item defines the portion of the concealment problem that a layout-blind fold can address COMPLETELY, and that is its central value to this project. Every technique here -- tag-block smuggling, variation-selector smuggling, zero-width binary encoding, bidi reordering, homoglyph substitution -- is a property of the code point sequence and is detectable with no rendering, no computed style and no geometry. Combined with item 13's channel analysis, the layout-blind defensive envelope becomes concretely statable: (a) channel exclusion removes roughly 70% of deployed injections (headers, comments, JSON-LD, metadata) by node type and tag; (b) Unicode screening removes or flags 100% of encoding-level concealment, exactly and deterministically; (c) inline-style-attribute string inspection catches the portion of rendering-based concealment that is declared inline; and (d) colour/contrast and occlusion concealment remain structurally out of reach and require the actuator-side peripheral described in items 32 and 13. The important unmeasured quantity is how the encoding-level class compares in prevalence to the rendering-based class -- item 13's 1.2-billion-URL study could not see encoded injections at all because its detector was English keyword matching, so the true split is unknown and could be substantial in either direction. Two further exposures specific to this class. First, the measured compliance rates for invisible instructions (up to 47.4% with tools) are an order of magnitude above those for visible hidden text (0.2-8.0%), so per-instance this is a far more dangerous class even if it is rarer. Second, TOOL ACCESS TRIPLES SUSCEPTIBILITY (47.4% with tools versus at most 16.9% without), which means an agentic design is materially more exposed than a read-only one and that the exposure grows precisely as the system becomes more useful.
provenance_carrying: Screening produces exactly the kind of per-node fact a provenance scheme should carry: a flag recording that this node's text contained tag-block characters, or unbalanced bidi controls, or mixed scripts, along with counts and the Unicode version used. Because the trie key already supplies the address, attaching the flag is free, and because the operations are exact the flag is trustworthy rather than probabilistic. This is the highest-quality provenance signal available anywhere in this research set, and it should be surfaced to the model inline alongside the content it qualifies -- a model told that a passage contained hidden characters can treat it accordingly, and a model told nothing cannot.
roundtrip_safety: Central and easily botched. Normalisation is idempotent (NFC(NFC(x)) = NFC(x)), which makes normalise-serialise-parse-normalise a fixed point and gives a free correctness check. Stripping is NOT idempotent-safe in the sense that matters: it is destructive, so the round trip is lossy and the original cannot be recovered unless the removed content is recorded. That is a further argument for FLAG-AND-RECORD over silent strip: keep the original in the capture, apply the sanitising transform in the projection, and record what the transform removed, so the round trip is lossy only in the derived artifact and the stored one remains exact. Escaping interacts too: a sanitiser that runs before HTML escaping and one that runs after can disagree, and invisible characters inside attribute values survive several escaping schemes intact.
token_budget_and_ordering: Small direct effect, one useful indirect one. Invisible characters cost tokens -- often disproportionately, since tag-block and variation-selector code points are rare and tokenise poorly, so a smuggled payload can consume many tokens while displaying as nothing, which is both a cost and a detection signal (a node whose token count greatly exceeds its visible character count is anomalous, and that comparison is a cheap mechanical check requiring no Unicode tables at all). On ordering: a per-node sanitisation flag should be emitted INLINE with the content it qualifies rather than in a summary, for the same reason as every other provenance marker -- given the position-bias findings of item 30, a caveat placed early and content placed late means the caveat is not attended to.
representation_cost: Negligible. The flags are a few tokens per affected node and affected nodes are rare. The stored cost is a small per-node record. The computational cost is linear scanning plus a table lookup, with the bidiSkeleton fast path avoiding the expensive route for LTR-only text. There is no meaningful budget argument against doing this on every node of every capture.
what_could_be_adopted: Six things, and this is the most directly implementable item in the research set. (1) A SINGLE NORMALISATION POINT: NFC at ingestion, before any hashing or key construction, applied identically on every path, with the Unicode version recorded. This alone prevents a class of duplicate-key and re-anchor-failure bugs that would otherwise appear months later with no obvious cause. (2) A SCRIPT-AWARE SANITISATION PROFILE built on UTS39 rather than on the common ad-hoc recipes: strip the Tags block and orphaned variation selectors outright; strip U+200B and U+FEFF; PRESERVE U+200C and U+200D and instead flag anomalous runs using a joining-context test; handle bidi by balance-checking and boundary-terminating per UAX9 HL4 rather than deleting; detect homoglyphs via UTS39 skeletons and restriction levels rather than substitution. (3) FLAG-AND-RECORD, NEVER SILENT STRIP: keep the original in the capture, transform only in the projection, and attach a per-address record of what was removed or flagged. (4) SCREEN ATTRIBUTES AND OUTPUT, not only text nodes and input. (5) THE TOKEN-COUNT-VERSUS-VISIBLE-LENGTH ANOMALY CHECK as a cheap, table-free tripwire that catches encodings the code-point rules have not enumerated. (6) TOKENISER-LEVEL FILTERING for the local model, which the Reverse CAPTCHA authors identify as the most robust mitigation and which is achievable precisely because the model is local -- a genuine advantage of this project's architecture over a hosted-model pipeline. Explicitly NOT to be adopted: the widely-published strip-all-zero-width recipe, which corrupts Indic, Persian, Arabic and emoji text; NFKC as a storage form; and any assumption that this class is rare, given that its prevalence has never been measured and the one large-scale study was structurally blind to it.
constraint_violation_ledger: structure_agnosticism: ADOPTABLE AS-IS, and it is the cleanest fit in the entire research set. Every operation here is a decidable property of a code point sequence, defined by a published standard with a reference implementation. Set membership in the Tags block, bidi class, script property, normalisation form and skeleton equivalence involve no classifier, no learned model, no page-structure assumption and no judgement about what a region means. There is nothing to reject. no_layout_in_the_fold: ADOPTABLE AS-IS -- no rendering is required for any detection. The one nuance worth stating: determining what a human ACTUALLY SEES under bidi reordering is a display question, but detecting that reordering controls are present, and computing bidiSkeleton to compare visual and logical order, are both pure string operations, so even the visually-defined attack is handled inside the fold. o_delta: ADOPTABLE AS-IS at node granularity, with named exceptions -- cross-node split payloads (the fundamental evasion, not node-local by construction), bidi controls whose effect crosses node boundaries, a Unicode version bump forcing an O(store) rescan, attribute screening needing attribute-mutation records rather than characterData records, output screening being outside the DOM delta entirely, and content in closed shadow roots or canvas being unscreenable. Naming these is what makes the screening guarantee falsifiable. no_mocks: ADOPTABLE AS-IS -- real standards data, real reference implementations, exact and testable. The MODEL SUSCEPTIBILITY figures are NEGATIVE ORACLE ONLY for this project: five hosted frontier models were tested and no small open-weight model was, and item 13's separate finding that small models are roughly tenfold more susceptible to visible injections suggests the 47.4% figure is a floor rather than a ceiling for a local 7-8B model. closed_shadow_roots_stay_closed: NO CONFLICT; text inside closed roots is simply unscreenable and belongs in the declared-incompleteness set. OVERALL VERDICT: adoptable as-is and should be built first. It is the only injection defence in this research set that is exact, deterministic, reproducible, script-invariant when done properly, geometry-free, and cheap -- and it covers the concealment class that a layout-blind design can address completely, which makes it the natural complement to the channel exclusion of item 13 and to the actuator-side rendered-flag of item 32. The one substantive risk is doing it naively and corrupting non-Latin text, which is a solved problem if UTS39 is followed rather than improvised.
governance_signal_handling: No interaction with robots.txt, Content Signals, ai.txt, AIPREF, Web Bot Auth or HTTP 402 -- this layer operates on text after retrieval. One adjacent observation: given item 13's finding that thousands of in-the-wild injections are site operators identifying or protecting against AI readers, some invisible-character payloads are plausibly of the same defensive character, and the same policy applies -- detect and surface as an observed access-preference signal attached to the origin rather than silently obeying or silently discarding.
legal_basis_and_pii_posture: Minimal direct relevance. Two notes. Silent sanitisation modifies stored third-party content, so a capture that has been stripped is no longer an accurate record of what was published -- which matters if captures are ever used as evidence of what a site said, and is another argument for storing the original and transforming only in the projection. And invisible characters are a covert channel that could carry personal data through a pipeline undetected in either direction, so output screening has a data-protection rationale as well as a security one.
